rv.q: The problem is that, like the ship itself, the play goes nowhere.
Dogstar deserves credit for its originality, in how it walks a tonal tightrope few could pull off.
Both witty and heart-rending, this Conrad-esque tale delivers laugh-out-loud humour and a startlingly surreal twist.
DOGSTAR is a quirky oddity with a few flaws but surprising charm.
However, despite top-notch acting from the three male leads, Dogstar is simultaneously too strange and not strange enough to warrant its 90-minute running time.
If you can forgive the static quality of the plotting, then this is an enjoyably ghostly excursion on a cold winter evening.
A strong cast did their best with what they were given, but what they were given was all over the place.
The three actors work fantastically well, both individually and as a trio.
An engaging, thought-provoking and powerful human drama.
It’s completely gripping and you spend an hour and a half completely absorbed by their world.
Daisy Hall is an author of promise who is well served by cast and director of this fascinating glimpse into nineteenth century whaling life.
If that is the message, it could be delivered in a funnier package with a bit more dramatic tension.
Dogstar is a work that feels immediately authentic in the layering of the characters' interactions and the conflicts and connections between them.
Imaginative, thought provoking and a bit bizarre, “Dogstar” is a bracing breath of fresh air, but it could do with having a somewhat clearer idea of where it is heading.

cn.t: Hall's dark comedy about icebound whalers delivers sharp humor and strong performances, but critics divide over a surreal twist that either deepens or derails the narrative, leaving the play as trapped as its characters.
